n: David and the leaders set apart the families of Asaph, Heman and Jeduthun to “prophesy” with instruments. Inspired music was seen as a form of prophecy—declaring God’s truth and praise.

f.g: To proclaim God’s word and praise through inspired song.
Set apart for a special assignment.

n: Asaph’s four sons served under their father’s direction, following the king’s arrangements.

f.w: according to the order of the king

n: Jeduthun’s six sons served under him, prophesying with the lyre in thanks and praise.

f.w: to give thanks and to praise the LORD

n: Heman’s fourteen sons are named. Read together, the last nine names in Hebrew sound like a short prayer-poem: “Be gracious to me, LORD… you are my God… I have magnified and exalted [your] help… I have spoken visions.”
Heman was the king’s seer, and God blessed him with fourteen sons and three daughters—a sign of divine favor. His family “lifted up the horn,” exalting God or Heman’s honor.

f.g: An idiom for increasing strength or honor; here perhaps of praising God.

n: All of them made music in the Lord’s house under their fathers, using cymbals, harps and lyres, according to the king’s directions. Families served together.

f.w: under the hands of their father
f.g: Taught and directed by their fathers—music passed down through families.

n: There were 288 trained musicians in all—twenty-four groups of twelve.
They cast lots for their turns of duty, young and old, teacher and student alike. In God’s service, all stand on equal footing.

f.g: The master the same as the student.

n: The first lot fell to Joseph of Asaph’s family and the second to Gedaliah of Jeduthun’s. Each course had twelve musicians.

f.g: “The LORD is great”; a son of Jeduthun.

n: The third lot went to Zaccur, Asaph’s eldest listed son.
The fourth lot went to Izri of Jeduthun’s family.
The fifth lot went to Nethaniah, a son of Asaph.
The sixth lot was the first to fall to Heman’s family, through Bukkiah.
The seventh lot went to Jesharelah, Asaph’s fourth son—completing Asaph’s four courses.
The eighth lot went to Jeshaiah of Jeduthun’s family.

f.g: A form of the name Isaiah, “the LORD saves.”

n: The ninth lot went to Mattaniah, a son of Heman. By this point all three music families are well represented.
The tenth lot went to Shimei, a son of Jeduthun not named in verse 3—making Jeduthun’s six sons complete.

f.g: Jeduthun’s sixth son, missing from verse 3’s list of names.

n: The eleventh lot went to Azareel of Heman’s family.
The twelfth lot went to Hashabiah of Jeduthun’s family—the halfway point of the twenty-four courses.
The thirteenth lot went to Shubael, a son of Heman.
The fourteenth lot went to Mattithiah, the last of Jeduthun’s sons to be assigned.

f.g: “Gift of the LORD”; also a Levite musician in 1 Chronicles 15:18, 21.

n: From the fifteenth lot onward, every course falls to Heman’s large family, beginning with Jeremoth.
The sixteenth lot went to Hananiah, whose name means “the LORD is gracious”—the first words of the name-prayer in verse 4.

f.g: “Be gracious, O LORD” or “the LORD is gracious.”

n: The seventeenth lot went to Joshbekashah, whose name may mean “sitting in hardship.”

f.g: Possibly “dwelling in difficulty”—part of the poetic sequence of names.

n: The eighteenth lot went to Hanani, “be gracious to me.”

f.g: “Be gracious to me”; a name also borne by a later prophet (2 Chronicles 16:7).

n: The nineteenth lot went to Mallothi, “I have spoken.”

f.g: Possibly “I have uttered” or “I have spoken.”

n: The twentieth lot went to Eliathah, “you are my God.”
The twenty-first lot went to Hothir, “he has given abundantly.”
The twenty-second lot went to Giddalti, “I have magnified.”
The twenty-third lot went to Mahazioth, “visions”—recalling that this music was considered a kind of prophecy.
The last lot went to Romamti-ezer, “I have exalted help.” The twenty-four courses of singers now match the twenty-four courses of priests, a complete order of worship.
